neighbors.heading: let your yes be yes
neighbors.text: Today Israel's leaders kept an oath, even after learning it was won by a trick. Catholics hold a spoken word sacred too. Jesus taught: "But let your speech be yea, yea: no, no." The Church teaches that God's name must never be used to back a lie, and that a promise made before him binds.
neighbors.difference: Joshua's leaders swore by God's name and stood by it. Jesus asked his followers to need no oath at all, just a plain yes; the Church still allows an oath for serious reasons, like in court.
neighbors.shared: a word you give is a word others can lean on.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:37 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2147, 2150, 2154 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: an empty dipper
neighbors.text: Today a promise held even when keeping it cost something. Buddhists guard their word as training. The Buddha once showed his son Rahula a dipper with a little water in it, then tipped it out: that's how empty the practice becomes of someone who lies on purpose without shame. Not lying is one of the five precepts.
neighbors.difference: Israel's leaders kept the oath because they had sworn by God, and breaking it would shame his name. Buddhism doesn't swear by a God; truthful speech is a precept you take on to train your own mind.
neighbors.shared: the truth you keep keeps you, too.

neighbors.heading: verify it first
neighbors.text: Today the tribes nearly went to war over an altar, until someone went and asked. The Qur'an gives the same counsel: "O ye who believe! If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did." The next verses call believers to make peace between quarreling brothers.
neighbors.difference: In Joshua, the tribes hear of the altar and gather for war, then send Phinehas and the leaders to ask face to face. The Qur'an makes checking a report a standing rule for believers, before anyone acts.
neighbors.shared: ask before you strike; the story may not be what you think.

neighbors.heading: not the thing, the reading of it
neighbors.text: Today an altar looked like betrayal, and turned out to be a plea: our children belong too. The Stoic Epictetus put the lesson in one line: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The tribes' fear came from their reading of a pile of stones. One honest conversation changed the reading.
neighbors.difference: In Joshua, peace comes when the eastern tribes answer in God's name and the others say the Lord is among them. Epictetus puts the work in your own judgments: you check your opinion, with or without a God.
neighbors.shared: the story in your head deserves one honest question first.

neighbors.heading: why call her less?
neighbors.text: Today Deborah, a judge, chose to call herself "a mother in Israel." Sikhs honor that word too. Guru Nanak sang that we are born of woman, befriended and married through woman, and that through her the generations go on. Then he asked: why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?
neighbors.difference: Deborah's song honors one woman who rose to lead in a dark time. Guru Nanak's hymn speaks of every woman, against a habit of looking down on women, and says only the True One is beyond being born of one.
neighbors.shared: honor the ones who bring us into the world.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Asa di Var (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let your mother be a god to you
neighbors.text: Today Deborah chose a word from home and called herself "a mother in Israel." Hindu teaching holds that word high too. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends students home with a few lines to live by, and the first is: let your mother be as a god to you. Then the father, the teacher, and the guest.
neighbors.difference: Deborah's "mother" describes how she leads a whole people: care before command. The Upanishad's line is about how each child honors their own mother, a duty of the home.
neighbors.shared: a mother's care deserves a place of honor.

neighbors.heading: not by birth
neighbors.text: Today Hannah sang of the poor raised out of the dust. Buddhists tell of the Buddha turning birth-rank upside down too. Called an outcast by a proud man, he answered that no one is an outcast by birth, and no one noble by birth: by deeds one becomes an outcast, by deeds a noble one.
neighbors.difference: In Hannah's song, God does the lifting, by his own hand. In the Buddha's teaching, no one lifts you: your own actions make you high or low, and anyone can walk the path.
neighbors.shared: where you start doesn't decide where you belong.

neighbors.heading: the lowly lifted up
neighbors.text: Today Hannah sang that God raises the poor from the dust and seats them with princes. Christians sing a song that echoes hers. When Mary, pregnant with Jesus, visits her cousin Elizabeth, she sings: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things."
neighbors.difference: Hannah sings over Samuel, the son she prayed for, and of a king not yet born. Christians hear Mary's song, the Magnificat, as praise for Jesus, whom they believe is the promised king; Jewish tradition doesn't read it that way.
neighbors.shared: nobody is too low to be lifted.

neighbors.heading: what you agree to attend to
neighbors.text: Today a boy learned one sentence: "Speak; for Thy servant heareth." Not a request, just attention. The psychologist William James saw how much rides on that: "My experience is what I agree to attend to." What we listen for shapes who we become. Samuel had to learn to turn toward a voice he first mistook for an old man's.
neighbors.difference: Samuel listens for God, a voice that comes from beyond him and carries a message. James describes how any mind works: attention picks what we notice, whatever we believe lies behind it.
neighbors.shared: listening well is a choice you can practice.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology, ch. 11 (William James 1890)

neighbors.heading: the ear of your heart
neighbors.text: Today Eli taught a boy to answer, "Speak; for Thy servant heareth." Catholic monks begin with listening too. The Rule of St. Benedict opens with one word, listen, and asks the reader to bend the ear of the heart to a teacher's words. Benedictine monks and nuns have lived by that Rule for centuries.
neighbors.difference: Samuel hears God call his name in the night, directly. Benedict's listening is mostly patient and daily: to scripture, to the abbot, to the community, where Catholics believe God speaks too.
neighbors.shared: the first step in any calling is listening.

neighbors.heading: a handful of rice
neighbors.text: Today a prince loved a shepherd "as his own soul" and gave him his own robe, asking nothing back. Hindus tell of a friendship like that. Sudama, a poor schoolmate of Krishna, came to his palace with only a little flattened rice to give. Krishna ran to meet him, washed his feet, and ate the rice with joy.
neighbors.difference: Jonathan and David are two people, the heir giving to the one who will rise. For devotees, Krishna is God himself, so Sudama's story also shows God treasuring the smallest gift given with love.
neighbors.shared: real friends give without keeping score.

neighbors.heading: love for your brother
neighbors.text: Today Jonathan loved David "as his own soul." Muslims keep a saying of the Prophet Muhammad that sounds close: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Another hadith counts two people who love each other for God's sake among those God will shade on the Day of Judgment.
neighbors.difference: Jonathan's love is told as one friendship, sealed with a covenant between two men. The hadith makes it a measure of faith for every believer, owed to anyone they call brother or sister.
neighbors.shared: want for a friend what you want for yourself.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Faith (paraphrase) · Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith of the seven given shade (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: call the lame to the feast
neighbors.text: Today a king sent for a lame man who expected punishment, and gave him a seat at his table, always. Jesus taught a table like that: "when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee."
neighbors.difference: David seats Mephibosheth out of chesed, the loyal love he owes his friend Jonathan. Jesus asks for a table where the guests have no claim at all, and says God will repay it.
neighbors.shared: a seat at the table can change a whole life.

neighbors.heading: everyone sits on the floor
neighbors.text: Today a lame man, sure he'd be punished, was given a place at the king's table for good. Sikhs keep a table open to everyone. In the langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara, people of any faith or rank sit side by side and eat the same simple meal. Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked even an emperor to eat there first.
neighbors.difference: David's table honors one man for his father's sake, a king choosing his guest. The langar has no host deciding who's worthy: everyone, even an emperor, sits on the same floor as an equal.
neighbors.shared: a shared meal says: you belong here.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of the langar, Guru Amar Das and Akbar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: bless, and curse not
neighbors.text: Today a man threw stones and curses at a fleeing king, and David said: let him curse. Catholics hear a call like that in Paul's letter: "Bless them that persecute you: bless, and curse not." And on the cross, Jesus prayed for the men putting him to death: Father, forgive them.
neighbors.difference: David holds back partly because he thinks the Lord may have sent the curse, and on his deathbed he doesn't forget Shimei. Catholics are asked to go past restraint, to wish good on the one who curses.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to answer every stone that's thrown.

neighbors.heading: a gift not taken
neighbors.text: Today David let an insult go by without needing to win. Buddhists tell of a man who came and abused the Buddha to his face. The Buddha asked: if you offer guests food and they don't take it, whose is it? Mine, the man said. Then this abuse, the Buddha said, I don't accept. It stays with you.
neighbors.difference: David lets the curses fall because maybe the Lord sent them, and hopes God will repay him with good. The Buddha simply declines the gift, so anger finds no home in his own mind.
neighbors.shared: an insult only lands if you pick it up.

neighbors.heading: increase me in knowledge
neighbors.text: Today Solomon asked God for a listening heart, not riches. Muslims know Solomon, Sulayman, too. The Qur'an tells of David and Solomon judging a dispute over a field, and says: "And We made Solomon to understand." It also teaches a short prayer anyone can say: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge."
neighbors.difference: In 1 Kings, Solomon is a king who asks for a listening heart. In the Qur'an, Sulayman is honored as a prophet, and his understanding is a gift named in God's own voice.
neighbors.shared: wisdom starts with asking to understand.

neighbors.heading: wise enough to know
neighbors.text: Today the new king called himself a little child, and asked to be able to hear. Socrates said something close. Told by the oracle that no one was wiser than him, he went questioning people famed for wisdom, and concluded: maybe I'm wiser only in this, that I don't think I know what I don't know.
neighbors.difference: Solomon asks God for wisdom and receives it as a gift. Socrates looked for it by questioning people, and found that admitting what you don't know is where it begins.
neighbors.shared: a humble mind has room to learn.

neighbors.heading: by listening
neighbors.text: Today God wasn't in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in "a still small voice." Sikh teaching prizes quiet listening too. In the Japji, Guru Nanak praises listening: by listening, he sings, sorrow and wrongdoing are erased. He names the quiet hours before dawn as the time to meditate on the True Name.
neighbors.difference: Elijah hears a voice that comes to him and asks him a question. Sikh teaching speaks less of a voice than of the Name, God's presence already within, found by quieting the mind's noise.
neighbors.shared: the quiet is sometimes where the voice is.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji Sahib, pauris 4 and 8-11, Ang 2-3 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: hidden in the heart
neighbors.text: Today the noise came three times, and God wasn't in it; then came a voice quiet enough to miss. Hindu teaching listens inward too. The Katha Upanishad says the Self, smaller than small and greater than great, is hidden in the heart of every creature, seen by one who grows free of craving and grief.
neighbors.difference: For Elijah, God speaks from outside him, and he wraps his face in his cloak. In the Upanishad, what's found in the heart is the deepest Self, which some Hindu schools teach is one with Brahman.
neighbors.shared: some truths only come when we're still.

neighbors.heading: the robe and the bowl
neighbors.text: Today a teacher was taken up, and his student picked up the cloak that fell. Buddhists tell a passing-on story too. In the Platform Sutra, the Fifth Patriarch of Chan secretly gives his robe and bowl to Huineng, a poor, unlettered worker from the rice mill, as a sign that the teaching now rests with him.
neighbors.difference: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, from the God of Elijah. In Chan the robe is only a sign; the teaching passes mind to mind, and the sutra says the robe itself stopped being handed on.
neighbors.shared: what a teacher gives you, you carry forward.
neighbors.sources: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, chapter 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: commit thou to faithful men
neighbors.text: Today Elisha picked up his teacher's mantle and struck the water, and it parted again. Christians keep a chain like that. The apostle Paul writes to his young student Timothy: "the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also."
neighbors.difference: Elisha receives Elijah's spirit in one dramatic moment, with a whirlwind and fire. Paul's handing-on is slow and ordinary, person to person, carried along, Christians believe, by the Holy Spirit.
neighbors.shared: every teacher was once somebody's student.

neighbors.heading: perpetual peace
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah said war is learned, so it can be unlearned. The philosopher Immanuel Kant hoped so too. In his essay Perpetual Peace he proposed, among other steps, that standing armies should in time be abolished, and that free nations join in a league bound by law. He laid it out as practical steps, not only a hope.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah's peace comes when the nations go up to learn God's ways from Zion. Kant built his case on reason, law and self-interest, a peace people could reach whatever they believed.
neighbors.shared: peace takes work, like iron beaten at a forge.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace, preliminary article 3 and second definitive article (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: war never again
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah pictured weapons beaten into farm tools. Catholics have carried that hope into the world's halls. In 1965 Pope Paul VI stood before the United Nations and pleaded: no more war, war never again. The Catechism calls everyone to pray and work to be freed from war, and names peace the work of justice.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah's peace arrives in the last days, as nations come to learn at the Lord's mountain. The Church still allows a nation to defend itself, under strict conditions, while pressing for peace now.
neighbors.shared: every peace begins with someone setting down a weapon.
neighbors.sources: Pope Paul VI, address to the United Nations, 1965 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2304, 2307-2309 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: father, and mother
neighbors.text: Today God said that even if a mother forgets her nursing child, "yet will I not forget thee." Hindus call on God as mother too. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says: I am the father of this world, the mother, the one who holds it up. Hindu devotion also prays to the Divine Mother, as Durga, as Lakshmi, or simply as Ma.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah uses a mother as a picture, then says God's love holds even where a mother's fails. In Hindu devotion, God may be worshipped as Mother herself, not only compared to one.
neighbors.shared: you are held more closely than you know.

neighbors.heading: more merciful than a mother
neighbors.text: Today God promised to remember, even if a nursing mother could forget. The Prophet Muhammad used that very picture. Seeing a woman among captives find her baby and hold it to her breast, he asked: would she throw her child into a fire? No, they said. God, he answered, is more merciful to His servants than she is to her child.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah speaks to a people in exile, God's promise to Zion. The hadith speaks of every servant of God, and all but one chapter of the Qur'an open with God's names, the Beneficent, the Merciful.
neighbors.shared: nobody is forgotten by the One who made them.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Good Manners (paraphrase) · Qur'an 1:1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: ye did it unto me
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah said the fast God wants is bread for the hungry and a home for the poor. Christians hear Jesus say it this way: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in." Whatever you did for the least of these, he says, you did for me.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah ties caring for the poor to a fast day and God's command. Jesus places himself in the hungry person, so Christians see serving them as serving him.
neighbors.shared: an empty stomach next door is a holy errand.

neighbors.heading: earn, and share
neighbors.text: Today the prophet said a fast means little if the hungry stay hungry. Sikh teaching makes sharing daily. Guru Nanak wrote that one who eats what he earns by honest work, and gives some of it away, recognizes the path. Sikhs name three daily pillars: work honestly, remember God, and share what you have.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah reshapes a fast day the people already keep. Sikh teaching doesn't center on fasting; it puts sharing into every ordinary day, at home and in the gurdwara's free kitchen.
neighbors.shared: your bread is meant to reach someone else's table.

neighbors.heading: living water
neighbors.text: Today God called himself "the fountain of living waters," left behind for cisterns that leak. Catholics hear that spring in John's Gospel. At a well, Jesus tells a Samaritan woman: "he that shall drink of the water that I will give him, shall not thirst for ever." Catholics see that water in baptism and in the Holy Spirit's gift.
neighbors.difference: In Jeremiah the fountain is the God of Israel, and the cisterns are idols and foreign powers. Catholics believe Jesus himself offers that living water, as the Son of God, which Jewish tradition doesn't hold.
neighbors.shared: the deepest thirst needs a spring, not a bucket.
neighbors.sources: John 4:13-14 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 694 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: thirst like a creeper
neighbors.text: Today people dug hard at cisterns that couldn't hold water. Buddhists have a word for that endless digging: tanha, thirst. The Dhammapada says: "The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest." Every cistern filled, and still thirsty.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah's answer is to return to God, the living spring. The Buddha points to no fountain outside: the thirst itself is seen clearly and let go, and that letting go is the peace.
neighbors.shared: the things we chase can't always hold what we pour in.

neighbors.heading: in the hearts
neighbors.text: Today Jeremiah heard a promise: God's teaching written not on stone but "in their hearts." Muslims carry their scripture inside too. The Qur'an calls itself "clear revelations in the hearts of those who have been given knowledge." Children and adults learn it by heart, and one who memorizes all of it is honored as a hafiz.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah pictures God writing the Torah inward, so no one needs teaching. For Muslims the writing within happens through people too, verse by verse, by memory and recitation of the Qur'an.
neighbors.shared: words you carry inside go everywhere you go.

neighbors.heading: the moral law within
neighbors.text: Today the teaching moved from stone to the heart. The philosopher Immanuel Kant wrote of two things that filled him with growing wonder the more he thought about them: "the starry heavens above and the moral law within." For Kant, right and wrong aren't only rules outside us; reason finds them already inside.
neighbors.difference: In Jeremiah, God does the writing, and the law within is God's own teaching. For Kant the moral law comes from reason itself, though he believed it also pointed toward God.
neighbors.shared: deep down, we can know what's right.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Critique of Practical Reason, conclusion (Abbott 1889)

neighbors.heading: washed by the Name
neighbors.text: Today Hosea gave his people words to come home with: return, and take words with you. Sikh scripture also speaks of washing a stained heart. In the Japji, Guru Nanak sings: when hands and feet are muddy, water washes them; when the mind is stained by wrongdoing, it is washed by love of the Name.
neighbors.difference: Hosea's words are a confession said aloud, standing where the offering once stood. For Sikhs, the cleansing comes through remembering God's Name with love, more than through naming each wrong.
neighbors.shared: the way back can start with a few words.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji Sahib, pauri 20, Ang 4 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: come back to me
neighbors.text: Today Hosea's word was shuvah: return. Hindu scripture holds the door open too. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that even someone who has done great wrong, if they turn to him with a whole heart, should be counted as good, for they have resolved rightly. Soon, he says, they become righteous and find lasting peace.
neighbors.difference: Hosea calls a whole people back to their covenant with God, with words as their offering. Krishna speaks to each person, and the turning he praises is single-minded devotion.
neighbors.shared: it's never too late to turn around.

neighbors.heading: toward all that lives
neighbors.text: Today God asked Jonah whether he shouldn't pity a great city, "and also much cattle." Buddhists practice that wide care on purpose. The Metta Sutta asks for kindness toward every living being, weak or strong, seen or unseen, near or far, the way a mother would guard her only child with her life.
neighbors.difference: In Jonah the mercy is God's, and Jonah is asked to see it. In the Metta Sutta, loving-kindness is a practice you grow in your own heart, toward every being, without a God at the center.
neighbors.shared: mercy grows wider when we stop measuring who deserves it.

neighbors.heading: the older brother
neighbors.text: Today Jonah sulked because God forgave a city he wanted punished. Jesus told of someone like that. When a wasteful son comes home and his father throws a feast, the older brother "was angry, and would not go in." The father goes out to him: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine."
neighbors.difference: Jonah's book ends with God's question about a foreign city and its animals. Jesus' story is about a family and a son coming home, and Christians hear in the father God's welcome to every sinner.
neighbors.shared: mercy for someone else isn't taken from you.

neighbors.heading: one word to live by
neighbors.text: Today Micah boiled it all down: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God." Confucius was asked the same kind of question: "Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?" He answered: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others."
neighbors.difference: Micah's three steps end in walking with God. Confucius's rule is about how people treat each other; he grounded goodness mostly in human relationships.
neighbors.shared: a good life fits in a sentence you can carry.

neighbors.heading: on these two
neighbors.text: Today Micah put the whole of the good in three verbs, and the Talmud says he summed up the Torah. Catholics hear Jesus do the same. Asked for the greatest commandment, he answered with two: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself. "On these two commandments dependeth the whole law and the prophets."
neighbors.difference: Both of Jesus' commandments come from the Torah, in Deuteronomy and Leviticus. Catholics receive them from Jesus, whom they believe is God made man; Micah's three steps come from a prophet.
neighbors.shared: the whole of it fits in a few honest words.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 22:37-40 (Douay-Rheims; verse 40 quoted) · Babylonian Talmud, Makkot 24a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: cook for more than yourself
neighbors.text: Today Boaz had grain dropped on purpose, so a poor stranger could gather it with her dignity whole. Hindu scripture warns against keeping the harvest to yourself. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the good eat what remains after offering, but those who cook only for themselves eat sin. Another old teaching: let the guest be as a god to you.
neighbors.difference: Boaz goes past the gleaning law, and does it quietly so Ruth isn't shamed. The Gita frames sharing as part of sacrifice: food offered and shared keeps the world's give-and-take turning.
neighbors.shared: leave room in your harvest for someone else.

neighbors.heading: on the harvest day
neighbors.text: Today Boaz told his reapers to drop extra handfuls for a stranger to glean. The Qur'an speaks of the harvest too. After naming gardens, date palms, olives and pomegranates, it says to eat of the fruit, "and pay the due thereof upon the harvest day." Muslims give zakat, a set share of wealth and crops, to people in need.
neighbors.difference: Boaz's kindness goes beyond the law, hidden so Ruth keeps her dignity. Zakat is one of Islam's five pillars, a duty with set amounts, and Muslims also give freely beyond it, called sadaqa.
neighbors.shared: what grows in your field was never only yours.

neighbors.heading: why hast thou forsaken me
neighbors.text: Today Job cursed the day he was born, and scripture kept every word. Christians remember a cry like that from the cross. Near his death, Jesus called out the opening of a psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Christians hear in it that even despair can be spoken to God, out loud.
neighbors.difference: Job's cry stands alone, a whole chapter with no answer. Jesus' words quote Psalm 22 from the Jewish scriptures, and Christians read his cry inside the story of his death and rising.
neighbors.shared: your hardest words can still be a prayer.

neighbors.heading: did You feel no pain?
neighbors.text: Today Job's rage stayed in the holy books, uncut. Sikh scripture holds a cry like it. When invaders struck the land and people cried out in agony, Guru Nanak sang to God: so much suffering, and did You feel no pain? His hymns about that invasion are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, word for word.
neighbors.difference: Job demands an answer for his own suffering, and his friends' explanations fail. Guru Nanak cries out for a whole people, and his hymns hold that cry alongside acceptance of God's will, the Hukam.
neighbors.shared: honest anguish has a place in front of God.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 360, Rag Asa, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: remember, you are dust
neighbors.text: Today Kohelet said all is hevel, breath: real, but impossible to hold. Catholics wear a reminder like that. On Ash Wednesday, a priest marks ashes on the forehead, often with words from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." It begins Lent, forty days of prayer, fasting and giving.
neighbors.difference: Kohelet looks at fleeting life and says: so eat your bread with joy, now. Catholics hold that the ashes point toward Easter, and to a life they believe lasts beyond this breath.
neighbors.shared: knowing life is short can make it sweeter.

neighbors.heading: all things pass
neighbors.text: Today the Preacher said everything we chase is breath: it can't be held. The Buddha taught that too, and called it anicca, impermanence. The Dhammapada says: "'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity."
neighbors.difference: Kohelet's breath points back toward a life lived under God, enjoyed while it lasts. The Buddha goes further: even the self is passing, and letting go of clinging ends suffering.
neighbors.shared: you can love what you can't hold onto.

neighbors.heading: hold fast together
neighbors.text: Today Kohelet said two are better than one, and "a threefold cord is not quickly broken." The Qur'an reaches for a rope too: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." The Prophet Muhammad described believers as a building whose parts hold each other up, and laced his fingers together.
neighbors.difference: Kohelet's cord is mostly human, friends who lift and warm each other, though some readers hear God as the third strand. In the Qur'an, God's rope comes first, and holding it is what binds believers together.
neighbors.shared: no one should have to fall alone.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 3:103 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith of the building (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: without friends
neighbors.text: Today Kohelet saw a man working alone, never asking who it was for, and called it breath. Aristotle said something close. In his Ethics he writes that without friends no one would choose to live, even having every other good. Friends keep the young from mistakes, care for the old, and help the strong do fine things: two going together.
neighbors.difference: Kohelet weighs friendship against a life that's only breath, and some readers hear God as the third strand. Aristotle grounds it in human nature: we're made to live with others.
neighbors.shared: two are stronger than one, and that's good news.

neighbors.heading: the ambrosial hours
neighbors.text: Today, in the middle of a lament, came a line of hope: mercies "new every morning." Sikh scripture meets the morning too. In the Japji, Guru Nanak names the amrit vela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, as the time to meditate on the True Name and its greatness. Each day starts again with remembering.
neighbors.difference: In Lamentations, morning brings God's mercies to a grieving people, and the grief stays all around it. In Sikh practice, the early morning is a daily discipline: rising to remember God's Name.
neighbors.shared: every morning is a fresh start.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji Sahib, pauri 4, Ang 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the light at dawn
neighbors.text: Today a lament found hope that comes fresh each morning. Hindu tradition greets the light too. The Gayatri, a prayer from the Rig Veda, is said at dawn: we meditate on the glorious light of the divine sun, Savitar; may it awaken our minds. Each morning, the prayer asks for the mind to be lit again.
neighbors.difference: Lamentations finds mercy renewed while the city still mourns. The Gayatri asks for light for the mind, a prayer for understanding, said at dawn and at other times of the day.
neighbors.shared: the dark doesn't get the last word; morning comes.

items.lessonTitle: They that be wise shall shine (Daniel 12:3)

neighbors.heading: like the moon from the clouds
neighbors.text: Today Daniel said the wise "shall shine as the brightness of the firmament." The Dhammapada uses light for wisdom too: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." In Buddhist teaching, the light comes when the clouds of carelessness part.
neighbors.difference: Daniel's wise shine because they teach many and turn them toward righteousness before God. The Dhammapada's light comes from a mind waking up from carelessness, through one's own effort.
neighbors.shared: a wise life gives light to others.

neighbors.heading: let your light so shine
neighbors.text: Today Daniel said those who turn many to righteousness will shine "as the stars for ever and ever." Jesus used the same picture. "Ye are the light of the world," he told his listeners. "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven."
neighbors.difference: Daniel's shining is promised for the end of days, for the wise who taught others. Jesus speaks of a light seen now, in ordinary good works, that points people to God.
neighbors.shared: the good you do can light someone else's way.

neighbors.heading: we learn by teaching
neighbors.text: Today the Levites stood among the people and explained the reading, so everyone understood. The Roman philosopher Seneca saw that teaching works both ways. Writing to a friend, he said that people learn while they teach. To make something clear for someone else, you have to understand it yourself.
neighbors.difference: In Nehemiah the teaching is God's law, and the goal is a whole people understanding it together. Seneca writes about philosophy shared between friends, learning that helps you live well.
neighbors.shared: understanding grows when it's shared.

neighbors.heading: how can I, unless someone shows me?
neighbors.text: Today Ezra read, and teachers "gave the sense," so no one was left with words they didn't get. Catholics keep that step too. In the Acts of the Apostles, an Ethiopian official is reading Isaiah, and Philip asks if he understands. How can I, he answers, unless someone guides me? At Mass, a homily follows the readings.
neighbors.difference: In Nehemiah, Levites explain God's law to the gathered people. Catholics trust the Church, from bishops to the parish priest, to give the sense of scripture, and Philip reads Isaiah as pointing to Jesus.
neighbors.shared: it's okay to ask for help understanding.
neighbors.sources: Acts 8:30-31 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 85, 1349 (paraphrase)
